tasks: 复盘一条寿险新闻对利率假设、退保率或新业务价值的影响。
写一段寿险产品利润来源拆解：利差、死差、费差、退保差。
记录一个值得跟踪的寿险公司战略动作。

items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.original_title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.rss_title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.rss_description: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges Claims ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:52 Hurricane Isaias shows how quickly claims surge after quiet periods, straining leaner teams to review complex restoration invoices thoroughly. October 29, 2026 Image Hurricane Isaias spun up in the Gulf of Mexico and made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm on Oct. 9, just two days after becoming the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, the latest first hurricane in more than a century. Its sudden arrival is a reminder of how quickly a quiet claims environment can change. For property claims teams, the workload extends well beyond the initial wave of reported losses. Damage to hotels, apartment communities, retail centers and industrial properties can lead to large restoration projects and complex invoices that arrive over the weeks and months that follow. Early modeled estimates of privately insured losses range from $1 billion to $2 billion (Verisk) to $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion (Moody's RMS). While AM Best expects it to be an earnings event for insurers rather than a capital event, the storm created a substantial uptick in work for claims and restoration teams. The aerial imagery firm Vexcel counted about 17,860 damaged structures across Florida, Alabama and Mississippi, including more than 3,100 with major damage. A high-rise condominium resort on Pensacola Beach lost windows across two towers, and an apartment complex in Milton, Fla., lost much of its roof. Damage like that becomes restoration projects, and restoration projects become invoices. Isaias follows a prolonged stretch of slower claims activity. Industry data puts commercial property claims at 710,000 in 2025, down from 910,000 in 2023. A separate measure, U.S. property claim assignments , fell 12% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 and ran 13% below the five-year average, extending a four-year decline. These are different Verisk datasets, but both point to a slower claims environment. More of the work that remains also arrives in bursts: catastrophe claims made up 43% of second-quarter volume, up from 34% five years earlier. No claims organization can staff indefinitely for a catastrophe-level workload during a stretch like this. Nor should it. Teams that have adjusted staffing and resources to match lower demand face a particular challenge: claims volume can rebound much faster than review capacity can be rebuilt. When restoration invoices pile up, those leaner teams face a difficult trade-off. Bills can wait for a thorough audit, extending claim cycle times, or move through with less scrutiny, increasing the risk of leakage. Automation offers a way to absorb more work without having to rebuild the entire manual review operation. The surge also has a long tail. When Hurricane Sally struck the same stretch of coast in 2020, Florida insurers had closed about two-thirds of residential claims six weeks later, but only 13% of commercial property claims. Hurricane Ian made landfall in Florida on Sept. 28, 2022. In the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation's March 4, 2025, snapshot , 96% of the 789,066 reported Ian claims were closed. Yet 6,628 of the 32,850 commercial property claims remained open nearly two and a half years after the storm. Those figures do not establish whether the delays involved coverage, reconstruction, invoice review, or disputes. They do show how long commercial claims work can continue after the initial surge. The bottleneck moves as the claim progresses An initial wave of assignments is only the beginning. Adjusters must address coverage, communicate with insureds, inspect damage, review scopes and estimates, and coordinate recovery. Restoration invoices arrive as work progresses, often while those adjusters are still managing both new and existing claims. Large restoration projects can involve multiple crews, weeks of drying equipment, substantial material charges, and several subcontractors. The resulting invoices can be complex even under normal conditions. When many arrive together, claims teams face two pressures at once: more invoices to review and more work required to review each one thoroughly. An invoice is not simply a total to approve. Time-and-materials bills can require checking labor hours and classifications, equipment usage and duration, agreed rates, materials, subcontractor charges, markups, and arithmetic. A reviewer may need to compare the invoice with supporting records and the work performed. That takes time, and the work does not become less necessary because the team has fewer people available. Both delayed reviews and unsupported payments carry consequences for the insured, the carrier, and the restoration contractor waiting to be paid. Adding more reviewers can help, but it takes time to find, train, and coordinate them. It also raises the cost of handling a temporary spike. The more useful question is which repeatable parts of review can be completed consistently without requiring a few more hours of specialist time for every additional invoice. How automation can absorb a surge AI-enhanced automation can help teams review restoration invoices faster by extracting and sorting line items and running calculations to identify charges that need a closer look. During a surge, these capabilities support consistent, thorough review. AI can help turn invoice documents into organized data, while programmed audit rules check calculations and compare charges with agreed rates or benchmarks. The adjuster or specialist still has to consider the work performed, evaluate the findings, and resolve disagreements. Automation reduces the manual checking that precedes those decisions. Rest-Assured has pioneered the use of AI-enhanced automation in restoration invoice auditing. Property insurers have used the platform to audit nearly $1 billion in property restoration invoices, uncovering documented findings to guide claims professionals through review and resolution. Measure the effect on the claim The right measure is not merely how fast an audit comes back. Claims leaders should look at the time from invoice receipt to a documented review, how long exceptions take to resolve, the rate of confirmed findings, the cost per review, and whether payment disagreements are cleared sooner. Those measures show whether faster processing is actually helping the claim move toward resolution. What to put in place before the invoices arrive Mitigation invoices begin arriving within weeks of landfall, and larger reconstruction bills follow for months. That gap is the time to prepare. Some insurers are already using automation to take on the time-intensive parts of invoice review, putting them in a better position to handle the next surge. A few decisions made now can keep review from becoming the bottleneck later: Confirm the rate agreements, pricing guidelines, and benchmarks reviewers will apply, including how post-storm pricing will be evaluated. Set one intake path for restoration invoices and define the supporting documentation each one needs. Identify which repeatable review steps, such as line-item extraction, arithmetic and rate checks, can be automated. Decide which findings can be resolved routinely and which require an adjuster or specialist. Decide in advance where overflow review goes if volume exceeds internal capacity. Claims teams cannot maintain catastrophe-level staffing through every quiet period. They need a review process that can expand when demand returns. Automating time-intensive invoice checks can help leaner teams absorb a surge without forcing a choice between longer cycle times and greater leakage. Restoration invoice auditing does not have to be a bottleneck, and keeping claims moving does not have to mean letting invoices pass through without scrutiny. Source notes Verisk ClaimSearch Trends Report, 2025 Year-end Analysis , p. 4. Commercial property claim counts are not directly comparable to the separate XactAnalysis assignment measure. Verisk Quarterly Property Report, April–June 2026 , pp. 3–4. Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, Hurricane Ian catastrophe claims data , as of March 4, 2025. items.extracted_text: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges | Insurance Thought Leadership Skip to main content Claims Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges Hurricane Isaias shows how quickly claims surge after quiet periods, straining leaner teams to review complex restoration invoices thoroughly. Jeff Esper October 29, 2026 Hurricane Isaias spun up in the Gulf of Mexico and made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm on Oct. 9, just two days after becoming the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, the latest first hurricane in more than a century. Its sudden arrival is a reminder of how quickly a quiet claims environment can change. For property claims teams, the workload extends well beyond the initial wave of reported losses. Damage to hotels, apartment communities, retail centers and industrial properties can lead to large restoration projects and complex invoices that arrive over the weeks and months that follow. Early modeled estimates of privately insured losses range from $1 billion to $2 billion (Verisk) to $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion (Moody's RMS). While AM Best expects it to be an earnings event for insurers rather than a capital event, the storm created a substantial uptick in work for claims and restoration teams. The aerial imagery firm Vexcel counted about 17,860 damaged structures across Florida, Alabama and Mississippi, including more than 3,100 with major damage. A high-rise condominium resort on Pensacola Beach lost windows across two towers, and an apartment complex in Milton, Fla., lost much of its roof. Damage like that becomes restoration projects, and restoration projects become invoices. Isaias follows a prolonged stretch of slower claims activity. Industry data puts commercial property claims at 710,000 in 2025, down from 910,000 in 2023. A separate measure, U.S. property claim assignments , fell 12% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 and ran 13% below the five-year average, extending a four-year decline. These are different Verisk datasets, but both point to a slower claims environment. More of the work that remains also arrives in bursts: catastrophe claims made up 43% of second-quarter volume, up from 34% five years earlier. No claims organization can staff indefinitely for a catastrophe-level workload during a stretch like this. Nor should it. Teams that have adjusted staffing and resources to match lower demand face a particular challenge: claims volume can rebound much faster than review capacity can be rebuilt. When restoration invoices pile up, those leaner teams face a difficult trade-off. Bills can wait for a thorough audit, extending claim cycle times, or move through with less scrutiny, increasing the risk of leakage. Automation offers a way to absorb more work without having to rebuild the entire manual review operation. The surge also has a long tail. When Hurricane Sally struck the same stretch of coast in 2020, Florida insurers had closed about two-thirds of residential claims six weeks later, but only 13% of commercial property claims. Hurricane Ian made landfall in Florida on Sept. 28, 2022. In the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation's March 4, 2025, snapshot , 96% of the 789,066 reported Ian claims were closed. Yet 6,628 of the 32,850 commercial property claims remained open nearly two and a half years after the storm. Those figures do not establish whether the delays involved coverage, reconstruction, invoice review, or disputes. They do show how long commercial claims work can continue after the initial surge. The bottleneck moves as the claim progresses An initial wave of assignments is only the beginning. Adjusters must address coverage, communicate with insureds, inspect damage, review scopes and estimates, and coordinate recovery. Restoration invoices arrive as work progresses, often while those adjusters are still managing both new and existing claims. Large restoration projects can involve multiple crews, weeks of drying equipment, substantial material charges, and several subcontractors. The resulting invoices can be complex even under normal conditions. When many arrive together, claims teams face two pressures at once: more invoices to review and more work required to review each one thoroughly. An invoice is not simply a total to approve. Time-and-materials bills can require checking labor hours and classifications, equipment usage and duration, agreed rates, materials, subcontractor charges, markups, and arithmetic. A reviewer may need to compare the invoice with supporting records and the work performed. That takes time, and the work does not become less necessary because the team has fewer people available. Both delayed reviews and unsupported payments carry consequences for the insured, the carrier, and the restoration contractor waiting to be paid. Adding more reviewers can help, but it takes time to find, train, and coordinate them. It also raises the cost of handling a temporary spike. The more useful question is which repeatable parts of review can be completed consistently without requiring a few more hours of specialist time for every additional invoice. How automation can absorb a surge AI-enhanced automation can help teams review restoration invoices faster by extracting and sorting line items and running calculations to identify charges that need a closer look. During a surge, these capabilities support consistent, thorough review. AI can help turn invoice documents into organized data, while programmed audit rules check calculations and compare charges with agreed rates or benchmarks. The adjuster or specialist still has to consider the work performed, evaluate the findings, and resolve disagreements. Automation reduces the manual checking that precedes those decisions. Rest-Assured has pioneered the use of AI-enhanced automation in restoration invoice auditing. Property insurers have used the platform to audit nearly $1 billion in property restoration invoices, uncovering documented findings to guide claims professionals through review and resolution. Measure the effect on the claim The right measure is not merely how fast an audit comes back. Claims leaders should look at the time from invoice receipt to a documented review, how long exceptions take to resolve, the rate of confirmed findings, the cost per review, and whether payment disagreements are cleared sooner. Those measures show whether faster processing is actually helping the claim move toward resolution. What to put in place before the invoices arrive Mitigation invoices begin arriving within weeks of landfall, and larger reconstruction bills follow for months. That gap is the time to prepare. Some insurers are already using automation to take on the time-intensive parts of invoice review, putting them in a better position to handle the next surge. A few decisions made now can keep review from becoming the bottleneck later: Confirm the rate agreements, pricing guidelines, and benchmarks reviewers will apply, including how post-storm pricing will be evaluated. Set one intake path for restoration invoices and define the supporting documentation each one needs. Identify which repeatable review steps, such as line-item extraction, arithmetic and rate checks, can be automated. Decide which findings can be resolved routinely and which require an adjuster or specialist. Decide in advance where overflow review goes if volume exceeds internal capacity. Claims teams cannot maintain catastrophe-level staffing through every quiet period. They need a review process that can expand when demand returns. Automating time-intensive invoice checks can help leaner teams absorb a surge without forcing a choice between longer cycle times and greater leakage. Restoration invoice auditing does not have to be a bottleneck, and keeping claims moving does not have to mean letting invoices pass through without scrutiny. Isaias insured loss estimates: Verisk, $1 billion to $2 billion onshore (Oct. 13, 2026) Moody's RMS, $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion private market (Oct. 16, 2026). AM Best and Vexcel figures as reported by Insurance Journal, Oct. 15, 2026. Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, Hurricane Sally claims data, as of Oct. 26, 2020. items.title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.original_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_description: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/26/2026 - 17:11 Bill Gross recently announced a free database of AI-generated ideas for innovative companies, based on the 31 methodologies that he's developed over the past three decades and that have powered his Idealab incubator. The list of ideas — currently totaling a whopping 1,208,580 — may or may not contain an idea that you'll be able to turn into big bucks, but I think that exploring the database and interacting with the ideas is worth a bit of your time. Many of the notions I see for the insurance market are provocative. They can at least suggest where there are holes in insurance offerings today that you should work to fill, even if you don't launch the sort of standalone company that Gross would love to see join his pioneering incubator. Let's have a look. Here is a link to the database . And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. items.original_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_description: Buy or Build? Yes. Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:49 AI has lowered barriers to building custom insurance workflows, but integration and adoption remain the hardest parts of implementation. October 26, 2026 Image One of my takeaways from ITC Vegas this fall was that a lot of vendors are playing defense. A lot of carriers are looking at what AI can do now and asking some version of the same question: Hold on a minute, the world changed, so should we just build everything ourselves? It's a fair question. The barriers to building have come down a lot in the last year, and the benefits of owning your own technology are real. When a convincing demo takes a couple of engineers instead of a sales cycle, the old reasons to buy start to look pretty thin. I suppose I'm not the most neutral person to ask. I've spent the last decade building and running Clearcover , an AI-native carrier, and now Dearborn Labs , an AI-native software development firm built specifically for insurance; if anyone was going to tell you to build everything, it would probably be me. But when people ask me whether to buy or build, my answer is...yes. We have components of our system that we bought and didn't build, and we're fine with that. We build more than we buy, though, and more every day. Is "yes" a dodge? Maybe a little. Mostly it's that buy vs. build was never one decision. Every carrier already runs a mix of both, workflow by workflow. And even the build half of my answer comes with an asterisk. Where should the line sit? The choices sit along a spectrum, made one workflow at a time, and lately the mix has been shifting toward build. That makes sense to me, and I'd expect it to keep shifting for as long as building keeps getting cheaper. Buy what's already solved well. If a problem looks roughly the same at every carrier, and someone has spent years getting good at it, there isn't much to gain from building your own version, and the time and money are better spent elsewhere. But that list gets shorter every month. Build the workflows where being different is the point, like how you triage a new claim or decide which risks to write. Buying those means working the same way as everyone else who bought the same thing, which probably isn't what you were going for. Where exactly that line falls depends a lot on the carrier and its lines of business, which is why a single company-wide decision on buy vs. build usually ends up wrong somewhere. The asterisk What qualifies as building, because you can put a demo together, is usually the smallest portion of the work. AI can change how a claim moves and which decisions get made without a person ever opening the file, but the systems underneath that workflow rarely change, or at least they rarely change quickly. Not everybody is doing a rip-and-replace of their whole company to launch a new AI workflow. A new claims-intake workflow still has to post to your core system and set reserves the way your actuaries expect, and an underwriting workbench still has to read from policy admin and write its decisions back. None of that shows up in a demo. The interface is mostly a solved problem now, and that's good news. The hard part is the wiring underneath it. Most of the AI conversations I have with carriers wind up being about traditional software engineering. That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

The executives were speaking during Arch Capital Group’s third-quarter earnings call last week. You can read more about Arch’s Q3 2026 results over at our sister publication Reinsurance News . Arch Capital has been active in the insurance-linked securities (ILS) and third-party reinsurance capital market for some years now, with this business expanding of late and most of this activity being understood to sit within its Arch Re division. The Arch third-party and ILS capital platform includes risk-sharing arrangements such as reinsurance sidecars, its sponsorship of catastrophe bonds and mortgage insurance-linked securities, the development and management of other ILS structures such as funds to enable investors to access risks it underwrites, as well as acting as a fronting service provider to certain ILS market participants or investors. It’s a broad-based offering, one we understand to be growing in stature and in the amount of third-party capital being managed for investors, which presumably is driving attractive fee income for the company. But it is not a business activity that is discussed with any regularity by the firm’s management team. Given where we are in the market cycle and perhaps due to Arch Capital’s activities in ILS and managing or facilitating third-party investor capital growing in stature, it’s perhaps notable that the latest earnings call saw a good deal more discussion of this business activity than we have typically seen in the past. Nicolas Papadopoulo, CEO of Arch Capital Group, commented on this a number of times during the Q3 2026 call. Discussing the reinsurance business unit, Papadopoulo explained, “Gross premiums written declined approximately 8% compared with the same quarter last year, reflecting abundant reinsurance capacity, particularly in property and short-tail lines. Consistent with our cycle management approach, we are reducing participation where returns no longer meet our objectives and increasingly leveraging third-party capital to manage net exposure and optimise returns on our own capital. “We will not chase growth for the sake of growth. We will remain patient and deploy capital where pricing and terms and conditions appropriately reflect the underlying risk. Our objective is not to become an index of the overall market. “Our global reach, underwriting expertise, and third-party capital platform allow us to take advantage of opportunities as they emerge and to construct a portfolio that delivers our required risk-adjusted returns.” Clearly Papadopoulo sees the third-party capital platform as a beneficial input to Arch’s underwriting and capital decision-making, something that often becomes all the more relevant in cycle management. Asked specifically about what Arch is seeing in terms of private capital interest in reinsurance, Papadopoulo said, “Third-party capital, it is a helpful tool for us, I think for the industry in general. As pricing goes down, it is a capacity that has a lower cost-of-capital, and the industry has been using it to provide solutions to brokers and insureds. “Arch is doing that, on the property side it has been there for a while. The supply comes and goes, as a carrier we have to be able to manage that. But I think it is an interesting and valuable tool to have. On the casualty side, on the reinsurance side, it is a little newer and untested. The question is, who has the tail risk in those structures, that is still a question.” Further discussing casualty opportunities, Arch’s CEO said that the most promising may be on the insurance side, while on casualty reinsurance he commented, “The role of third-party capital, it adds another dimension to the supply on the reinsurance side. So I think it contributes to more supply, which makes it more difficult to find growth.” One of the analysts on the earnings call asked the Arch management about operational expenditure, noting that the OpEx ratio has improved, but asking what might be a driver for that. Arch Capital’s CFO François Morin responded to this question, “The nuance or maybe the difference for reinsurance is there’s certainly some profit commissions on third-party capital that come into play here, and it’s been a relatively benign cat environment the last couple of years. Is that a run rate? That’s for you guys to decide whether in a more normalised cat year we would probably have slightly less in terms of profit commissions. “The rest, again, our teams are working hard to manage the expense base and kind of have that line up with the growth in premium. That’s again, just back on the profit commissions, that may be the one thing on reinsurance that is something to think about.” Which clearly spells out that the third-party capital business is driving positive income for Arch, which it helping to lower its expense ratio. Unfortunately the company does not break out the dollar value of the income generated through its third-party capital and ILS activities, but it’s reasonable to assume it is a meaningful enough amount and another valuable lever for the company’s earnings. Later in the call, one analyst asked how Arch might look to navigate the current soft cycle in reinsurance, to which CEO Papadopoulo stated, “We have different tools today than we had back then. If you look at our gross number and ceded number and net number on the reinsurance side, a large portion of our premium is already ceded to sidecars or third-party capital. “For us, the philosophy is to really manage the net portfolio and ultimately stay in front of our clients. We have a leadership position and really figuring out and working with third-party capital, which I mentioned have a lower cost-of-capital, to be able to find solutions for cedants and brokers. That’s how we see it.” Which shows the CEO and company recognise how third-party capital access and management can be an especially useful tool in cycle management. Finally, Arch Capital’s CEO Papadopoulo also made some comments on the outlook for reinsurance renewals and property catastrophe risks in particular. Papadopoulo commented, “Clearly, we expect some continued pressure on the short-tail book, catastrophe, excess of loss, and other property, which is a big part of the portfolio in reinsurance, a much bigger part than in insurance. That will put pressure on the top line. “But we like the market we are in, I think we are trading well. We have a big book, we have great brands, we are still finding opportunities and we also take underwriting actions as pricing is going down. You have to put all of this together and figure out where we are going to end up at 1/1. items.extracted_text: Global ILS expansion presents strategic capital opportunity for APAC: Howden Re - Artemis.bm Global ILS expansion presents strategic capital opportunity for APAC: Howden Re - Artemis.bm Global ILS expansion presents strategic capital opportunity for APAC: Howden Re 2nd November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Ahead of the Singapore International Reinsurance Conference (SIRC), executives from Howden Re and Howden Capital Markets & Advisory (HCMA) emphasized that regional cedents should incorporate alternative capital into their broader toolkits to negotiate deeper partnerships and maximize optionality as reinsurers seek growth across Asia-Pacific (APAC). In a commentary published ahead of the SIRC event, Howden Re’s Andy Souter, David Flandro, Nena Atkinson, and HCMA’s Bill Cooper discussed how reinsurance capital has drastically changed shape in recent years, with institutional investors, private credit, and ILS funds now backing vehicles from catastrophe bonds and sidecars to new Lloyd’s syndicates. While much of this activity remains centered in London and the United States, Howden Re argues it is already actively shaping the capacity, pricing, and partnerships available to cedents across APAC. The sharp rise in alternative reinsurance capital, so that deployed through insurance-linked securities, accounts for much of the scale of the shift. “Reinsurance capital has become much more diverse, with alternative capital now accounting for close to a quarter of the sector’s total capital base. Dedicated reinsurance capital is now well north of US$500bn, following a period of very strong sector profitability,” commented Nena Atkinson, Associate Director, Howden Re Strategic Advisory. Atkinson also underlined how the catastrophe bond market sits in the centre of that change. “Cat bonds are now a structural part of the market, and issuance continues to set new records in 2026,” Atkinson said. Last year, catastrophe bond issuance surpassed $20 billion for the first time, setting a record of $25.6 billion. 2026 has also been another exceptional year so far for the cat bond market, as total nine-month 2026 issuance managed to reach a new $18.9 billion high of risk capital. As we’ve alluded to in previous articles, with the cat bond market pipeline steadily building for the fourth-quarter of 2026, Artemis is already tracking what will mark only the second year where issuance of 144A catastrophe bonds and private cat bond deals has exceeded the $20 billion level. Analyse the catastrophe bond market using our charts and visualisations, which are kept up-to-date as every new transaction settles . Bill Cooper, Managing Director, Howden Capital Markets & Advisory, also underlined how investors are consistently reaching further across the market to expand their capital base. “Financial investors are now providing risk capital to a wider range of insurance vehicles and classes, in the form of sidecars and other structured capacity vehicles, such as reinsurance syndicates at Lloyd’s,” Cooper explains. The executives also emphasised that institutional and private capital is primarily entering the market through ILS and collateralised or private arrangements, with diversification being a large part of the appeal. David Flandro, Head of Industry Analysis and Strategic Advisory, added: “One attraction of ILS is that returns are broadly uncorrelated with broader financial markets. Property cat remains the main focus, although there is growing appetite across other perils and geographies, including casualty, specialty, cyber in particular, and APAC.” That diversification still has plenty of room for growth, as more than half of ILS deals in the market cover the US exclusively, while only 11% cover non-nat-cat perils. Importantly, Howden Re and HCMA acknowledges that the Lloyd’s market has also become a focal point for this capital as well. “Financial investors of various sizes and types have been very active in providing capital to businesses underwriting at Lloyd’s. There have been several high-profile examples of investors financing structured capacity vehicles such as reinsurance syndicates, but we have also seen an increasing number of credit and other private investors backing a range of syndicates,” explains Cooper. The syndicates themselves are continuously evolving, with Cooper emphasising the formation of multiple new Lloyd’s syndicates designed to facilitate single-cedent outwards reinsurance. However, this shift is what presents a key opportunity for APAC insurers and investors. “Lloyd’s is keen to see new proposals where the underlying risk broadens the footprint of the market, especially by geography. We believe this is a real opportunity for APAC insurers and investors,” Cooper added. This shift will fundamentally change how reinsurers view and approach the APAC region going forwards. Providing further clarity, Andy Souter, Managing Director, Head of APAC, Howden Re, stated that this will sharpen reinsurers’ focus on maintaining relevance and help re-evaluate the value they add to cedents. “As reinsurers seek growth opportunities, and ‘replacement demand’ for business lost to third-party capital, APAC will be a source of interest. It is a region where reinsurers typically assess that they are underweight, and where third-party capital use may be more tempered than elsewhere. That creates a drive to stay relevant and grow with clients in the region,” Souter continued. Interestingly, Souter also urges insurers to consistently keep track of the developments that form parts of a longer-term shift in how institutional capital participates in reinsurance, along with the opportunities this creates for alternative solutions. Foremost, the executive underlines the importance of not disregarding this development. “The default reaction shouldn’t be ‘not relevant to APAC’. The question is how we can use this capital as part of the capital toolkit, and how to balance various sources of capital to achieve optimal reinsurance and maximise optionality through the market cycle,” Souter said. This necessitates guidance encompassing both traditional capacity and alternative capital sources, integrating insight into global market developments with regional knowledge. Reinsurance pricing is consistently softening, and the relatively benign loss environment this year has supported further capital growth across both traditional and alternative sources, which Flandro states adds to supply during a time where demand has not increased to the same extent. However, higher risk premia in the capital markets provide an important counterweight and should, in theory, support a higher pricing floor. In the Asia-Pacific market, buyers are taking advantage of this situation to negotiate deeper strategic partnerships with reinsurers. “It is early days, but at a high level this should serve as a platform for exploring the best form of partnership with reinsurers. Not just terms and conditions, but strategies to maximise reinsurer relationships,” Flandro added. Prospectively, Atkinson sees the growth of alternative capital as structural, even if its deployment proves more cyclical. The ILS market has grown for roughly 15 years and is now viewed across the market as being an integral part of most cedents’ programme structures. “The exceptionally profitable period of the last few years has attracted capital into both the ILS and traditional sectors, and we are now seeing more capital chasing growth as pricing falls. A concern would be a situation where too much capital is chasing deployment and investors become less disciplined on price and risk selection,” Atkinson said. At the upcoming January 2027 renewals, Howden Re states that the additional capacity will add to an already well-supplied market and could also influence where pricing sits and how long the softening market lasts. “We still expect the pricing floor to be higher than in 2017, given higher interest rates, inflation and risk premia,” Atkinson added. “The capital reshaping reinsurance may be concentrated in London and the US, but its effects reach every region. For APAC insurers, understanding it is the first step to using it well, whether through new forms of capacity, deeper reinsurer partnerships or greater optionality through the cycle,” Howden Re said. items.extracted_text: Everspan to Sell Providence Washington Shell to RI’s Falvey Group Article 0 Comments Everspan Group, a specialty property/casualty insurance platform and wholly owned subsidiary of Octave Specialty Group, Inc., has agreed to sell the admitted shell company Providence Washington Insurance Co. (PWIC) to Rhode Island-based Falvey Insurance Group. New York-based Everspan said the sale is expected to improve operational efficiencies and increase its tangible book value by approximately $11 million. The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and required regulatory approvals. PWIC is a Rhode Island-domiciled insurance company that Everspan acquired in 2021. It is one of five property/casualty companies owned by Everspan. We believe Falvey is a natural home for the company and are pleased to see its legacy continue.” Falvey is a specialty insurance provider founded in 1995. Headquartered in North Kingstown, Rhode Island, the group acts as a managing general agent (MGA) and service provider for cargo, marine, supply chain, transportation and logistics risks Following the announcement of the agreement, AM Best placed under review with developing implications the Financial Strength Rating of A- (Excellent) and the Long-Term Issuer Credit Rating of “a-” (Excellent) of PWIC. items.extracted_text: Marine risk in Asia: From insurance capacity to risk capability - Commercial Risk As trade routes, supply chains and shipping technologies evolve, marine resilience increasingly requires more than insurance capacity. It depends on better risk insight, coordinated programme delivery and practical loss prevention. Asia sits at the centre of global trade. Its ports, manufacturing centres, energy projects and logistics networks connect producers and consumers around the world, making the efficient movement of goods critical to regional and global economic activity. The shipping industry has repeatedly demonstrated resilience in the face of disruption. But for shipping companies, cargo owners and logistics providers, a more complex operating environment is testing what resilience requires. Insurance capacity remains essential when cargo values, routes and exposures change. Yet capacity alone does not prevent a loss, resolve a disrupted shipment or restore a complex supply chain. Those outcomes depend on risk insight, practical loss prevention, coordinated insurance programme delivery and effective claims handling. The pressures are both geopolitical and operational. Geopolitical tensions, including armed conflict, can alter strategic shipping routes, lengthen transit times, restrict port access and affect safety conditions with little warning. Longer voyage times, higher fuel costs and freight rates, and additional security requirements can have consequences far beyond the directly affected areas. Extreme weather, including drought, can disrupt ports, canals, terminals and inland transport. Meanwhile, AI data-centre growth is increasing the volume and value of cargoes such as semiconductors, power equipment and copper. Supply chains are being redesigned as the industry seeks to adopt alternative fuels, automation, electrification and greater digitalisation, introducing new operational risks. Larger ships, greater concentrations of cargo value and complex salvage operations can amplify loss severity. Electric vehicles and lithium-ion batteries introduce additional risk considerations, while fewer practical route alternatives can compound disruption. Disruption can spread quickly through this concentrated and interconnected system. For businesses, resilience therefore means combining insurance capacity with broader risk capability. Interconnected risks across the cargo journey Marine risk has always been international, but the connections between risks are becoming more visible. According to the World Shipping Council, nine of the world’s 10 largest container ports are in Asia, handling a combined 303.62 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) in 2025. The region also contains major production hubs and critical trade corridors. UNIDO’s World Manufacturing Production and Trade Quarterly Report has highlighted strong growth in higher-technology industries and exports across the region. Alternative fuels and increasingly automated operations are also changing risk profiles across vessels, ports and supporting infrastructure. Battery-powered equipment and fuels including methanol and ammonia bring new considerations around fire, handling, training, storage and emergency response. Greater digital connectivity may improve efficiency, but it also increases reliance on technology and exposure to cyber incidents, digital-document fraud and technology-enabled cargo theft – an increasing risk. As demand grows for AI-related cargoes such as copper, semiconductors and datacentre equipment, criminal groups are increasingly using phishing, fraudulent identities, fabricated shipping documents and compromised transport systems to identify shipments, impersonate carriers and divert cargo. GPS spoofing and cloned telematics can further delay detection. Asia is also exposed to tropical cyclones, flooding, earthquakes, severe convective storms and extreme heat. The consequences extend beyond physical damage: delayed components can interrupt manufacturing, delay critical construction projects, affect contractual obligations and increase cargo accumulation. Recovery may also be delayed by shortages of specialist equipment, labour or alternative transport. Marine risk management must therefore consider the full journey of goods – from production and storage to loading, sea transit, discharge and final delivery – rather than viewing each stage in isolation. For businesses, this means understanding how disruption at one stage can affect cargo accumulation, operational continuity and recovery elsewhere in the supply chain. Global oversight, local delivery For cargo owners and shipping businesses operating across several markets, the challenge is to retain central visibility while ensuring that insurance arrangements meet local requirements and work in practice when a shipment or claim needs attention. Asia is not a single insurance or regulatory market. Requirements vary between jurisdictions, including rules on local policy issuance, taxes, certificates, claims handling and compulsory insurance. Local practices and market capacity may also differ. A well-designed multinational marine insurance and risk management programme can help businesses manage this complexity. It can combine a centrally-coordinated approach with local policies where required, aligning group-level risk management with local regulatory and operational needs. This can support central control, consistency and transparency across loss prevention, insurance coverage, shipment certificates and claims service. A master policy can provide a common framework for coverage and programme governance, but local implementation is equally important. A programme is tested not when it is placed, but when cargo is moving, a certificate is needed urgently, or a loss occurs in a jurisdiction far from the corporate risk management team. Better insight, stronger loss prevention The growing complexity of marine exposures is increasing demand for timely and meaningful risk information. For high-value or sensitive cargoes, loss prevention begins well before a shipment departs. It can involve reviewing packing and securing arrangements, lift plans, stowage, route selection, survey requirements, storage conditions and locations, and the controls applied by freight forwarders and contractors. Technology can support theft prevention as well as operational efficiency. End-to-end visibility across vehicles, trailers and cargo can help validate reported delays, route deviations or breakdowns against real-time information, supporting earlier identification of suspicious activity. Technology can also support robust carrier and subcontractor vetting, including independent checks of licences, insurance cover, fleet capacity, digital identity and transaction history. Technology, however, is an enabler rather than a substitute for expertise. Its value depends on using the information it provides to identify weaknesses and guide practical preventive action. Value beyond risk transfer In one example, an Asia-based trading company had experienced repeated cargo shortfalls. Following a review, AXA XL’s risk consulting team recommended targeted improvements to handling and control processes. The measures helped to halve shortages per shipment, generating annual savings of more than US$700,000 (€602,000) for the client. Claims data, risk surveys and operational experience can help identify patterns that may not be apparent to an individual business, enabling preventive action before a larger loss develops. The speed and breadth of change in the maritime sector mean businesses need more than insurance capacity. They need clearer visibility of their exposures, stronger controls across supply chains, practical support in preventing losses and confidence that insurance programmes can respond consistently across borders. items.extracted_text: PERILS finalises industry loss estimate for Australia east coast SCS at AU $1.62bn - Artemis.bm PERILS finalises industry loss estimate for Australia east coast SCS at AU $1.62bn - Artemis.bm PERILS finalises industry loss estimate for Australia east coast SCS at AU $1.62bn 2nd November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Catastrophe data aggregator PERILS AG has published a fourth and final industry loss estimate for the Australia East Coast Severe Convective Storms (SCS) which affected the states of Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria in late October 2025, placing the insurance market loss at AU $1.62 billion, an 8% increase from the firm’s third loss estimate. Between October 26th and November 1st, 2025, Eastern Australia experienced an extended period of severe thunderstorms, with the most significant event impacting the greater Brisbane region in South East Queensland on October 26th. At the same time, a severe tornado caused extensive damage in Melbourne’s western suburbs on the same day. After a brief lull, another outbreak of severe storms struck South East Queensland as well as parts of northern New South Wales between October 31st and November 1st, 2025. PERILS’ initial loss estimate for this event was AU $1.108 billion, reported in December 2025. Then in February, the firm increased its industry loss estimate by 37% to AU $1.512 billion. Then in April, PERILS slightly lowered its insurance industry loss estimate for the event to AU $1.501 billion. Now, the final industry loss estimate for the event has increased by roughly 8% from the third loss estimate to AU $1.62 billion, PERILS has reported today. PERILS’ loss estimate is based on detailed loss data by postcode and property and motor hull lines of business collected from the majority of the Australian insurance market. According to PERILS, property losses contributed a staggering 87% of the total industry loss, while 13% were due to motor losses. The event predominantly impacted the state of Queensland, which experienced 94% of the total industry loss, while New South Wales and Victoria contributed 4.5% and 1.5%, respectively. Darryl Pidcock, Head of Asia Pacific & Cyber at PERILS, commented: “As Australia experiences the peak storm season, this event is a reminder of the widespread damage that severe convective storms can cause, especially along the east coast of Australia. “We continue to observe various factors driving industry losses such as an increase in vulnerable assets, especially with the growth of solar panel installations in Australia, and the impact of a warming climate. Australia is currently experiencing El Niño conditions which typically bring drier and hotter conditions to eastern Australia. Notwithstanding, the threat of convective storm activity is still very real as recent storm and flash flooding activity reminds us, especially during spring into early summer.” Pidcock continued: “We have observed more modest loss development in the last six months as insurers settled claims, with an 8% increase since our previous loss report, which is within expectations for this type of event.
